The Rise of Weather Wimpiness
            

            Floyd is making me believe more strongly in a Divine
Power: From the moment yesterday that I professed to you my belief that acts of
God are now invariably overhyped, this one began heading directly toward
metropolitan New York--toward me, I'm thinking, and my flip, callow hubris. The
kids' school canceled classes at 6:45 this morning, which has led me in turn to
try to weasel out of a book-reading-and-signing I'm supposed to do tonight. I
do think people are bigger weather wimps today than they were when we were
kids. (Canceling school because of rain?) But then, I was a kid in Omaha,
Nebraska, where weather wimpiness was literally unthinkable. In fact, extreme
weather is the most interesting part of life in Nebraska. (Extreme weather and,
briefly, when I was 4, Charles Starkweather, the real-life serial-murderer
Martin Sheen played in Badlands .) The one time, around 1967, that a
tornado actually touched down in our yard--a little tornado, but still--I was
away at summer camp. I have never regretted missing any event more.

response:
The Rise of Weather Wimpiness

Floyd is making me reconsider my belief in a Divine Power—perhaps not because of the storm itself, but because of how we now react to it. Since I recently confessed to you my growing skepticism that modern acts of God are invariably overblown, this one has been hurtling straight toward metropolitan New York—toward me, I suspect—serving as a kind of cosmic rebuke to my own youthful arrogance. This morning, the kids’ school canceled classes at 6:45, prompting me to quietly contemplate backing out of a book-reading and signing I’m scheduled for tonight. I can’t help but think people today are far more weather-averse than we were as children. (Canceling school for rain?) I grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where weather wimpiness was practically inconceivable. Extreme weather wasn’t just common there—it was the thrill of life. (And, briefly, the brief, chilling presence of Charles Starkweather, the real-life serial killer portrayed by Martin Sheen in *Badlands*, when I was four.) The one time a tornado actually touched down in our yard—small, but undeniable—I was away at summer camp. I’ve never regretted missing anything more.

        can also reveal a lot about the general role of microevolution in species divergence.
        Reinforcement provides a pathway toward the completion of the speciation process.

        roughly proportional to the genetic distance between the populations, reflecting the fact

        extensive hybridization may occur. This can result in fusion back into a single population,
        or in the swamping of one population's gene pool by the genes of the other (extinction).

You can also take advantage of an audio CD tour to give you background detail as you explore.
The collection is varied but most visitors come to see the works of the Dutch masters. Dutch painting of the 15th to 17th centuries are to be found in rooms 201 to 236 on the second floor. Among the collection are 20 works by Rembrandt, including The Nightwatch, properly entitled The Company of Captain Frans Banning Cocq and Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch. The work, which was commissioned by the company for its barracks, is remarkable for its lack of formality and very different from the accepted style of the day.
Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) is also well-represented, and his effective use of light can be clearly seen in The Kitchen Maid, painted in 1660, which is one of the gallery’s best-loved pieces. There are paintings by Frans Hals, the founding artist of The Dutch School, along with a collection of Dutch artists influenced or schooled by the masters.

response:
Enhance your visit with an audio CD tour, which provides insightful background as you explore the collection. While the gallery features a diverse range of artworks, most visitors are drawn to the celebrated works of the Dutch masters. Located on the second floor, rooms 201 to 236 house an exceptional selection of Dutch paintings from the 15th to 17th centuries. Among the highlights are 20 works by Rembrandt, including *The Nightwatch*—officially titled *The Company of Captain Frans Banning Cocq and Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch*. Commissioned by the civic guard for their meeting hall, this masterpiece stands out for its dynamic composition and informal vitality, marking a bold departure from the rigid conventions of the era.

Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) is also prominently featured, with his delicate handling of light and atmosphere on full display in *The Kitchen Maid* (c. 1660), one of the gallery’s most cherished works. The collection further includes pieces by Frans Hals, the founding figure of the Dutch School, as well as works by other Dutch artists shaped by the masters’ influence, offering a comprehensive view of the Netherlands’ golden age of painting.

response:
Some forms of animal suffering are shocking and undeniable—dogs forced into life-or-death fights for the entertainment of bloodthirsty gamblers; baby calves confined in cramped, dark stalls and deliberately underfed to produce tender "milk-fed" veal; porpoises accidentally drowned in tuna fishing nets. And each year, nearly 6 million companion animals are euthanized in shelters across the United States, many of them healthy and adoptable.

What is even more alarming is that over 30 million animals endure cruel, painful deaths annually—deaths that are entirely preventable.

In the face of such widespread suffering, the mission of The Humane Society of the United States has never been more urgent. Your support is essential to our work in ending animal abuse, neglect, and exploitation. Since 1954, we have dedicated ourselves to protecting animals through rigorous investigations, legal advocacy, and collaboration with law enforcement to hold perpetrators accountable. With your help, we can continue this vital work and create a world where no animal suffers needlessly.

response: Coach groups travel from near and far to explore the vibrant, colorful market, a bustling hub of commerce and culture. Just beneath the permanent market buildings, on the main Praça da República, a well-preserved section of the medieval castle walls stands as a testament to the town’s storied past—though severely damaged by the 1755 earthquake. Where does the term come from? Southerners pinned the label
on both the opportunistic and idealistic Northerners who packed their worldly
possessions into "carpetbags" during Reconstruction and moved to Dixie to enter
politics. A term of opprobrium, the word came from the Southerners' perception
that the newcomers represented the dregs of society, seeking nothing but easy
political gain. In particular, carpetbaggers were scorned for capitalizing on
the freed slaves' newly granted right to vote. Testifying before a
congressional committee in 1872, Alabama Democrat William M. Lowe explained, "A
carpetbagger is generally understood to be a man who comes here for office
sake, of an ignorant or bad character, and who seeks to array the negroes
against the whites."

            While the North won the
Civil War, the South won Reconstruction. By the late 1870s, Southern
"redeemers" (as they were admiringly called) got the federal government to
withdraw the troops that were safeguarding the rights of blacks. Meanwhile,
white supremacists regained control of state governments through fraud and
violence. Confederate apologists, who wrote the first round of histories of the
South, portrayed slavery as a benign, paternalistic institution (for more on
this topic, see "") and painted the carpetbaggers as venal and corrupt
interlopers.

response:
Where did the term "carpetbagger" come from? It originated during Reconstruction, when Southern whites used the word to describe Northerners—both opportunistic and idealistic—who migrated south, carrying their belongings in inexpensive carpetbags, in search of political advancement. Initially a term of scorn, it reflected the belief that these newcomers were morally and intellectually inferior, driven solely by self-interest and eager to exploit the newly enfranchised African American vote. As Alabama Democrat William M. Lowe testified before a congressional committee in 1872, a "carpetbagger" was generally seen as a man who came to the South "for office sake, of an ignorant or bad character," and who sought to incite racial division by pitting Black citizens against white ones.

Though the North had won the Civil War, the South ultimately reclaimed control of its destiny during Reconstruction. By the late 1870s, Southern "redeemers"—as they were proudly dubbed—had succeeded in persuading the federal government to withdraw military forces that had been protecting the rights of newly freed African Americans. With federal oversight gone, white supremacists reasserted power through intimidation, voter suppression, and outright violence. In the process, they reshaped the historical narrative: Confederate apologists, who wrote the earliest histories of the South, portrayed slavery as a benevolent, paternalistic system and cast the carpetbaggers as greedy, corrupt outsiders—figures of moral and political degradation.

**The New York Times Magazine**  
*March 21, 1999*  
*(Posted Thursday, March 18, 1999)*

The compelling cover story follows the troubling trajectory of Jim Kopp, the suspect in the 1998 murder of abortion provider Dr. Barnett Slepian. Once a "prayerful defender of life," Kopp evolved into an extremist willing to embrace violence—an evolution mirrored by broader shifts within the anti-abortion movement. From the nonviolent activism of Operation Rescue to the militant directives of the Army of God manual, the movement has increasingly embraced violent tactics. These strategies may be working: Between 1992 and 1996, the number of hospitals, clinics, and physicians offering abortions dropped by 14 percent.

Meanwhile, a profile examines Charlie Rose’s transition to *60 Minutes II*, asking whether his distinctive, conversational style—marked by thoughtful hesitation and a relaxed, almost stumbling charm—can succeed in a more fast-paced, results-driven format. The article suggests his success may hinge on his ability to set aside the very qualities that make him compelling.

In a separate feature, the revitalization of the Levi’s brand is explored. After losing ground to younger consumers in the early 1990s, Levi’s struggled to adapt to a cultural shift toward looser, more casual styles and to a new generation for whom shopping is an experience, not just a transaction. To reclaim relevance, the company is quietly re-entering youth culture through strategic sponsorships—such as concerts featuring Lauryn Hill—on-the-ground promotions like sidewalk chalkings and flyers, and high-profile commercials directed by Errol Morris, airing during popular shows like *Dawson’s Creek*.

Virilis data were obtained from non-coding regions with known or suspected cis-regulatory function. The data presented here represent a more random sampling of non-coding regions in the Drosophila genome. Conservation of non-coding sequences is typically interpreted as evidence of functional constraint. The assumption that conservation of non-coding sequences indicates functional constraint underlies most phylogenetic footprinting methods. This assumption was questioned by Clark [45]. Clark [45] proposed an alternative hypothesis for non-coding conservation based on heterogeneity in mutation rates. The alternative hypothesis proposed by Clark [45] involves mutational cold spots. To resolve the alternatives between functional constraint and mutational cold spots, the spatial distribution and conservation of spacing between CNCSs in the Drosophila genome were studied. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, CNCSs should occur randomly in non-coding DNA. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, the lengths of 'spacer intervals' between CNCSs should be exponentially distributed [46, 47]. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, there should be no tendency for the spacing between mutational cold spots to remain conserved between divergent Drosophila species. The reasoning for the lack of conservation in spacing between mutational cold spots is based on the rapid rate of DNA loss in unconstrained sequences in the Drosophila genome [48, 49].

HA-NFATp binds DNA alone and cooperatively with
          cJun/cFos
          To test the DNA binding activity of recombinant
          HA-NFATp and the ability to bind DNA cooperatively with
          cJun/cFos we performed DNase I footprinting. We used a
          DNA fragment from the human IL-2 promoter that contains a
          high affinity NFAT site (-45 NFAT site) and a composite
          element consisting of a low affinity NFAT site and a low
          affinity AP1 site, to which the DNA binding domain of
          NFAT has been shown to bind cooperatively with AP-1
          proteins [ 4, 11]. When increasing amounts of HA-NFATp
          were added to IL-2 DNA in the absence of cJun/cFos, the
          -45 NFAT site was protected from DNase I digestion, but
          as expected DNase I digestion of the composite element
          was unaffected (Figure 2, lanes 1-5). In other studies we
          found the observed equilibrium dissociation constant ( 
          obs K 
          D ) of recombinant HA-NFATp for a high
          affinity NFAT site (mouse IL-4 promoter) to be 1 nM (data
          not shown). cJun/cFos alone protected the AP-1 site of
          the composite element (Figure 2, lane 6). When increasing
          amounts of HA-NFATp were added to IL-2 DNA in the
          presence of cJun/cFos, clear protection of the entire
          composite site was observed (Figure 2, lanes 7-10). From
          DNase I footprinting studies (Figure 2and data not shown)
          we conclude that recombinant HA-NFATp binds DNA both on
          its own and in cooperation with AP-1 proteins (cJun/cFos
          and cJun/cJun).

CANDIDATE:
HA-NFATp binds DNA alone, as demonstrated by DNase I footprinting performed on a DNA fragment derived from the human IL-2 promoter, which contains a high affinity NFAT site at -45 and a composite element comprising a low affinity NFAT site and a low affinity AP1 site. When increasing amounts of recombinant HA-NFATp were added in the absence of cJun/cFos, the -45 NFAT site was protected from DNase I digestion, indicating direct binding, whereas the composite element remained unaffected. The observed equilibrium dissociation constant (obs K_D) of recombinant HA-NFATp for a high affinity NFAT site—derived from the mouse IL-4 promoter in other studies—was found to be 1 nM, though those data are not shown. In contrast, when cJun/cFos were present, they alone protected the AP-1 site within the composite element. Upon addition of increasing amounts of HA-NFATp in the presence of cJun/cFos, clear protection of the entire composite site was observed, indicating cooperative binding. DNase I footprinting studies, including those illustrated in Figure 2 and additional data not shown, support the conclusion that recombinant HA-NFATp binds DNA both independently and cooperatively with AP-1 proteins, specifically cJun/cFos and cJun/cJun. This cooperative interaction is further substantiated by references [4] and [11], which confirm the ability of the NFAT DNA binding domain to bind cooperatively with AP-1 proteins to the composite element. The conclusion regarding cooperative binding with AP-1 proteins is based on DNase I footprinting data and on information not presented in the visible results.

Indeed, the global transcriptional repressor
        PIE-1, the regulator of embryogenesis in 
        C. elegans , binds the histidine-rich stretch in CycT1, thus
        decoying P-TEFb away from RNAPII and blocking the elongation of transcription [30].
        These are exciting findings and suggest a plethora of future experiments, including the
        genetic inactivation of subunits of P-TEFb and isoforms of HEXIM1 in the mouse. Of special
        interest are questions as to where to place this mechanism of transcriptional regulation in
        the hierarchy of competing or complementary processes. What roles do different P-TEFb
        complexes play in the transcription of specific genes? How central will the regulation of
        P-TEFb be to cellular growth, proliferation, and differentiation, and what roles will it
        play in normal development and disease states? As to HIV, how can we use our knowledge of
        P-TEFb to slow down viral replication and/or to eliminate the state of proviral latency in
        the host?

CANDIDATE:
The global transcriptional repressor PIE-1 is a regulator of embryogenesis in C. elegans, binding the histidine-rich stretch in CycT1 to decoy P-TEFb away from RNAPII, thereby blocking transcriptional elongation. These findings are described as exciting, suggesting a plethora of future experiments, including the genetic inactivation of subunits of P-TEFb and the genetic inactivation of isoforms of HEXIM1, to be conducted in the mouse. There is special interest in determining where the mechanism of transcriptional regulation involving PIE-1 and P-TEFb is placed in the hierarchy of competing or complementary processes, and questions remain about what roles different P-TEFb complexes play in the transcription of specific genes. The centrality of P-TEFb regulation to cellular growth, cellular proliferation, cellular differentiation, normal development, and disease states is uncertain but under investigation. For HIV, there is interest in using knowledge of P-TEFb to slow down viral replication and to eliminate the state of proviral latency in the host, though the possibility of either approach is uncertain. The passage does not attribute any opinion to a specific person regarding the significance of these findings, though the term "exciting" is used.

By world
        standards, this racially varied society is a model of harmony.
        What will strike you first is the marvelous range of subtly
        different skin tones and facial features. The famous FWI women,
        inevitably wearing bright earrings and flashing colors, manage to be
        both graceful and sensuous as they walk. This is true even when they
        glide along country roads with large bundles balanced on their heads.
        Little girls learn this sure-fire posture-improver very early in
        life.
        In these already overpopulated islands, where Roman
        Catholicism is the predominant religion, the government provides an
        initial lump sum for each birth and a monthly support grant, allocation
        familiale, for each child. Because of the male exodus to France and
        elsewhere in search of jobs, women continue to outnumber men. More than
        half of 800,000 native islanders are children, and the mother is
        traditionally responsible for bringing them up, handling the money, and
        making key domestic decisions.

CANDIDATE:
On a global scale, this racially diverse society stands as a model of harmony. What immediately captures the eye is the remarkable spectrum of skin tones and facial features, each subtly distinct. The famed women of the FWI, invariably adorned with vibrant earrings and colorful attire, move with an effortless grace that is both elegant and sensual—even as they stride along rural paths, balancing large bundles on their heads with practiced ease. This poised, upright posture is a skill mastered from an early age, taught to little girls as part of their cultural inheritance.

On these already densely populated islands, where Roman Catholicism is the dominant faith, the government offers a one-time financial grant at birth and a monthly support payment, known as *allocation familiale*, for each child. Due to the ongoing migration of men to France and other regions in search of employment, women continue to outnumber men. With more than half of the native population—around 800,000 people—being children, the role of the mother remains central: she traditionally assumes responsibility for raising the children, managing household finances, and making key domestic decisions.

**The New York Times Magazine**  
*March 21, 1999*  
*(Posted Thursday, March 18, 1999)*

The compelling cover story follows the troubling trajectory of Jim Kopp, the suspect in the 1998 murder of abortion provider Dr. Barnett Slepian. Once a "prayerful defender of life," Kopp evolved into an extremist willing to embrace violence—an evolution mirrored by broader shifts within the anti-abortion movement. From the nonviolent activism of Operation Rescue to the militant directives of the Army of God manual, the movement has increasingly embraced violent tactics. These strategies may be working: Between 1992 and 1996, the number of hospitals, clinics, and physicians offering abortions dropped by 14 percent.

Meanwhile, a profile examines Charlie Rose’s transition to *60 Minutes II*, asking whether his distinctive, conversational style—marked by thoughtful hesitation and a relaxed, almost stumbling charm—can succeed in a more fast-paced, results-driven format. The article suggests his success may hinge on his ability to set aside the very qualities that make him compelling.

In a separate feature, the revitalization of the Levi’s brand is explored. After losing ground to younger consumers in the early 1990s, Levi’s struggled to adapt to a cultural shift toward looser, more casual styles and to a new generation for whom shopping is an experience, not just a transaction. To reclaim relevance, the company is quietly re-entering youth culture through strategic sponsorships—such as concerts featuring Lauryn Hill—on-the-ground promotions like sidewalk chalkings and flyers, and high-profile commercials directed by Errol Morris, airing during popular shows like *Dawson’s Creek*.

Coach groups travel from near and far to explore the vibrant, colorful market, a bustling hub of commerce and culture. In fact, there are two distinct markets: one dedicated to fresh produce, including fish, housed in a striking mock-Moorish hall, and a lively “gypsy market” located at the opposite end of the boulevard. Just beneath the permanent market buildings, on the main Praça da República, a well-preserved section of the medieval castle walls stands as a testament to the town’s storied past—though severely damaged by the 1755 earthquake. The ramparts offer panoramic views of the surrounding area, and nestled within the ancient stones is a modest but engaging local museum. Don’t miss several notable historic sites: the Igreja Matriz (São Clemente), a 13th-century Gothic church adorned with 18th-century azulejo tiles; the Convento da Graça, renowned for its exquisite Manueline portal; and the Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Conceição, a small church celebrated for its ornate Baroque altar and intricate ceramic tiles. Along the streets below the castle walls, the rhythmic clang of craftsmen shaping copper can often be heard—offering visitors a unique opportunity to purchase handcrafted wares directly from the artisans.

CANDIDATE:
Coach parties come from far and wide to shop at the colorful, bustling market.
There are actually two markets. Fresh produce, including fish, is sold in a mock-Moorish hall, while a “gypsy market” is held towards the opposite end of the boulevard. Just below the permanent market halls, on the main Praça da República, you’ll find a well-preserved section of the medieval castle walls (which were much damaged by the 1755 earthquake). The ramparts afford excellent views from the town, and set into the castle remains is a modest local museum. Also worth visiting are the Igreja Matriz (São Clemente), a 13th-century Gothic church with 18th-century azulejo tiles; the Convento da Graça, with a terrific Manueline portal; and Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Conceição, a small church prized for its Baroque altar and ceramic tiles.
In the streets directly below the castle walls, you may well hear the sounds of craftsmen beating copper — from whom you can buy direct.

            When my friend Ralph Cohen announced that his wife
was pregnant, I asked what path he hoped his child would follow. "It doesn't
matter," said Ralph. "If he's happy, I'll be happy." Then, after a thoughtful
pause he added, "My personal preference is shortstop. But anything he wants to
do is fine with me." Then, after a longer pause: "As long as it's in the
infield."

            That's the difference between ordinary altruism,
where you care about other people's happiness (though perhaps not as urgently
as you care about your own), and what I'll call "imperfect altruism," where you
reserve the right to care about how others achieve their happiness.

            We all feel altruistic toward our own future
selves. That's why we make current sacrifices for future rewards. But which
kind of altruists are we? Traditional economic theory says we're the ordinary
kind--we want to be happy in the future, though perhaps not as urgently as we
want to be happy in the present. David Laibson, a professor of political
economy at Harvard, is one of a few iconoclasts who disagree. Nobody doubts
that we are imperfectly altruistic toward others. Laibson argues that we can be
imperfectly altruistic toward ourselves. And just as imperfect altruism toward
your children can cause conflict in your family, imperfect altruism toward your
future self can cause conflict in your soul.

Where did the term "carpetbagger" come from? It originated during Reconstruction, when Southern whites used the word to describe Northerners—both opportunistic and idealistic—who migrated south, carrying their belongings in inexpensive carpetbags, in search of political advancement. Initially a term of scorn, it reflected the belief that these newcomers were morally and intellectually inferior, driven solely by self-interest and eager to exploit the newly enfranchised African American vote. As Alabama Democrat William M. Lowe testified before a congressional committee in 1872, a "carpetbagger" was generally seen as a man who came to the South "for office sake, of an ignorant or bad character," and who sought to incite racial division by pitting Black citizens against white ones.

Though the North had won the Civil War, the South ultimately reclaimed control of its destiny during Reconstruction. By the late 1870s, Southern "redeemers"—as they were proudly dubbed—had succeeded in persuading the federal government to withdraw military forces that had been protecting the rights of newly freed African Americans. With federal oversight gone, white supremacists reasserted power through intimidation, voter suppression, and outright violence. In the process, they reshaped the historical narrative: Confederate apologists, who wrote the earliest histories of the South, portrayed slavery as a benevolent, paternalistic system and cast the carpetbaggers as greedy, corrupt outsiders—figures of moral and political degradation.

South, portrayed slavery as a benign, paternalistic institution (for more on

interlopers.

Virilis data were obtained from non-coding regions with known or suspected cis-regulatory function. The data presented here represent a more random sampling of non-coding regions in the Drosophila genome. Conservation of non-coding sequences is typically interpreted as evidence of functional constraint. The assumption that conservation of non-coding sequences indicates functional constraint underlies most phylogenetic footprinting methods. This assumption was questioned by Clark [45]. Clark [45] proposed an alternative hypothesis for non-coding conservation based on heterogeneity in mutation rates. The alternative hypothesis proposed by Clark [45] involves mutational cold spots. To resolve the alternatives between functional constraint and mutational cold spots, the spatial distribution and conservation of spacing between CNCSs in the Drosophila genome were studied. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, CNCSs should occur randomly in non-coding DNA. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, the lengths of 'spacer intervals' between CNCSs should be exponentially distributed [46, 47]. Under a simple mutational cold-spot hypothesis, there should be no tendency for the spacing between mutational cold spots to remain conserved between divergent Drosophila species. The reasoning for the lack of conservation in spacing between mutational cold spots is based on the rapid rate of DNA loss in unconstrained sequences in the Drosophila genome [48, 49].

               Dear Prudie,
            

            
               I have a very close friend (we were in junior
high together in 1984) who seems to have just dropped out of society. He
doesn't look for work, having been let go from his last job. He rarely washes,
smokes and drinks too much (amongst other similar vices), and spends the time
he's not watching infomercials until 4 a.m., pining over a girl who broke up
with him long ago. He's living off unemployment, and that's going to run out
soon. 
               Oh, did I mention? He's living on my couch.
            

            
               To his credit, he's not hard to live with. He

food, and when he does he eventually replaces it. Plus, he's great company.
We've got very similar sense of humor and we have great conversations.

response:
Dear Prudie,

I’ve known my closest friend since junior high, back in 1984, and over the years, he’s become like family. Lately, though, he’s fallen into a troubling pattern. He hasn’t worked since being laid off from his last job, and despite his efforts, he hasn’t been able to reenter the workforce. He rarely showers, smokes heavily, drinks excessively, and spends his nights—often well past 4 a.m.—watching infomercials while obsessively replaying memories of a girl who broke up with him years ago. He’s now living off unemployment benefits, which won’t last much longer.

To my surprise—and honestly, my dismay—he’s been staying on my couch.  

That said, I have to admit: he’s not a burden. He keeps his space clean, respects my boundaries, and even replaces the food he eats. He’s also one of the most entertaining and thoughtful people I know—our shared sense of humor and deep conversations make time with him genuinely enjoyable.  

Still, I can’t help but worry. He’s adrift, and I’m starting to feel trapped between my loyalty to him and the growing sense that I’m enabling a downward spiral. What should I do?

My question—“Where would you rather be arrested: in the U.S. or Senegal?”—was not meant as an ad hominem attack on Amnesty International’s report. Rather, it was a response to the organization’s director, who claimed that the U.S. criminal justice system lags behind “the world community” in fairness. While I acknowledge that our system has flaws and that other nations offer valuable lessons, my broader point remains: people who argue that most countries are fairer than the U.S. would likely not actually want to be arrested, imprisoned, tried, or sentenced in most of them. The idea that fairness is universally prioritized in criminal justice is, at best, questionable.

I have learned with much interest that people envision solutions for
international characters data exchange with a wider point of view than
usually heard in the networking sphere.
I have been spending quite a time of my life with such problems.
I thought I could contribute with a small text explaining the way
I have finally come to think of the problem.
Nothing totally new, probably, but a different shed of light, maybe.
The text may sound theoretical at first. It is just terse. The ideas are
based on experience. They have been put to use in the field of 8-bit
characters. I participated to the design of Kermit multinational 8-bit
characters support and the TCP/IP network I work for is well on the way
towards the the same theory that every character on the communication
line is ISO 8859-1. Any exception to this, like translating EBCDIC directly
to PC code on one machine, is considered harmful to our internetworking,
even if convenient.
Every piece working towards a common well defined goal finally pays more
when all parts start to clutch than wandering for immediate interest.
And I hope that saying that my language is French will make the ideas
in a difficult to write text even more convincing, despite being short.

response:
I have long been fascinated by the way people approach the challenge of international character data exchange—not just as a technical problem, but as a broader systems issue. Having dedicated significant time and effort to this field, I feel compelled to share a concise reflection on how I now view the problem.

This text does not offer revolutionary ideas, but rather presents a fresh perspective—shaped by years of practical experience. The concepts, though expressed briefly and perhaps abstractly at first, are grounded in real-world application. They have already proven effective in the domain of 8-bit character handling: I contributed directly to the design of Kermit’s multinational 8-bit character support, and the TCP/IP network I work with is steadily adopting the principle that every character transmitted over the communication line should be ISO 8859-1 by default. Any deviation from this—such as direct EBCDIC-to-PC code translation on a single machine—is seen as harmful to interoperability, even if it offers short-term convenience.

Ultimately, progress comes not from isolated optimizations, but from aligning all components toward a shared, well-defined goal. When every piece works in concert, the collective benefit far outweighs the sum of individual gains.

And perhaps, in sharing that my native language is French—adding a layer of linguistic nuance to this brief yet complex text—I can lend it a touch of authenticity and depth, making its ideas more compelling, despite its brevity.

Navajo has long been touted by sociolinguists as a
language whose speakers maintain a great deal of language loyalty, that is, the
Navajo are reluctant to give up their heritage language. Yet the need to
establish a high-school Navajo class suggests that off the reservation, that is
exactly what young Navajo speakers are doing. The Hasidim of New York and the
Amish are two other groups known for preserving their speech--when, that is,
they maintain their social isolation from the mainstream. But once that
isolation is gone, language may soon follow.

            Cultural-loyalty movements like the class in Navajo
tend to spring up when cultural preservation is in danger, and their record of
success is not impressive. Here at the University of Illinois, we run special
sections of first- and second-year Spanish for Spanish-heritage students, and
the reason is that their Spanish is too weak to meet academic requirements.
That in turn means they may be able to speak Spanish (even that is often not
the case); but they can't read it well or write it fluently, and their grasp of
its grammar may be weak, since they haven't actually studied it as a language.
They may speak some Spanish, but they can't pass a test in it. Students also
use college language classrooms to try to recapture the heritage languages they
may have lost (for example, Hindi or Urdu), or ones they may never have
acquired (Yiddish).

response:
Navajo has long been celebrated by sociolinguists as a language marked by strong speaker loyalty—its communities are often reluctant to abandon their heritage language. Yet the growing need to establish high school-level Navajo language programs off the reservation suggests that many young Navajo speakers are, in fact, distancing themselves from their native tongue. Similarly, other culturally distinct groups such as the Hasidim of New York and the Amish are renowned for preserving their languages, but only so long as they remain socially isolated from the broader mainstream. Once that isolation ends, language preservation often follows suit.

Cultural-loyalty initiatives—such as heritage language classes—typically emerge when a language is under threat, yet their success rate remains limited. At the University of Illinois, for example, we offer specialized sections of first- and second-year Spanish tailored for Spanish-heritage students. The reason? Their spoken Spanish is often insufficient to meet academic standards. While some may speak the language informally, many lack the reading proficiency, writing fluency, and grammatical understanding required for academic success—because they have never formally studied Spanish as a language. As a result, they may speak some Spanish, but they cannot pass a language proficiency exam. These same classrooms also attract students seeking to reclaim heritage languages they never fully acquired—like Yiddish—or those they may have lost, such as Hindi or Urdu.

The answers some GAO evaluators gave may illustrate the range of
definitions surrounding case study methods.
To some GAO evaluators, the instance was an application of the
case study method, because we were looking at only a few sites or
because we could not generalize or because "actual subjects are
being used for analysis of a specific question." To some, the
instance was clearly not an application of the case study method,
because "we do not know if the instances are representative of the
universe," and "there doesn't appear to be enough done at each
site." To still others, it was not possible to tell whether this
was a case study because looking at instances was what we do in all
our methods, and there was no differentiation between this job and
a compliance audit.
The definitions given also varied greatly.

response: The varying responses from GAO evaluators highlight the wide range of interpretations surrounding case study methods. Some evaluators considered the instance a case study because it involved a limited number of sites, precluded generalization, or focused on actual subjects in the analysis of a specific question. Others rejected the label, arguing that the instances might not be representative of the broader population and that insufficient depth of analysis was conducted at each site. Still others found it impossible to determine whether the approach qualified as a case study, noting that examining individual instances is common across all evaluation methods and that this particular effort did not clearly differ from a compliance audit. These differing perspectives underscore the significant variation in how case study methods are defined and applied within the organization.

response:
Romney (1734–1802) is regarded as the third great master of portraiture in 18th-century England, ranking alongside Thomas Gainsborough and Joshua Reynolds. The gallery, renowned for its high profile, regularly hosts major traveling exhibitions—visitors are encouraged to check with the Tourist Information Centre for the latest program.

Housed in the beautifully renovated stable block of the estate, the museum features a series of vivid dioramas that bring to life Lakeland life and industry over the past two centuries. These displays celebrate the region’s skilled craftsmen, who played a vital role in the prosperity of Kendal and other Lake District towns, while also offering a comprehensive overview of the area’s economic development and the lasting impact of human activity on the landscape.

Near the railway station, the Kendal Museum of Archaeology and Natural History showcases an intriguing collection of Neolithic and Roman artifacts unearthed across the Lake District, alongside geological specimens and a remarkable array of taxidermied animals—both native to the region and from around the world.

Reality and Dreams shares its build with Memento Mori, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, and A Far Cry from Kensington, and it shares many of its features and many of its gestures with each of those works. Memento Mori is a flawless exploration of mortality, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie is a flawless exploration of hero worship, and A Far Cry from Kensington is a flawless exploration of literary politics. Not every member of a distinguished family is equally appealing; Branwell Brontë, for instance, drank and raved. Reality and Dreams is not Spark's most pleasant novel, though it features Tom Richards as its hero—a filmmaker who has a passion for controlling things and trouble distinguishing between his fictions and his real life, and who does his best to manipulate both. Tom Richards is hard to warm to.

They believe that resources for political activism on behalf of special interests are necessarily limited, and would prefer to allocate their financial support and emotional concern to protecting actual, real live human beings suffering actual, real live oppression, or the threat of such oppression. The speaker expresses a wish that the Catholic League, or any other group, showed concern about the fact that W. has presided over a state that executes people at an ungodly rate, a rate the speaker describes as particularly high, using the term "ungodly" (as it were) to emphasize its severity. While they can easily understand why someone would want to kill the murderer of a near and dear one, they state they cannot understand why someone would want to give the state the power to kill someone, even if the state is not abusing that power in a given case. The speaker believes that the state's power to kill will be abused, probably sooner rather than later, and cites the much-publicized racial statistics of the death penalty’s application as evidence that the death penalty is prone to abuse.

               Dear Prudie,
            

            
               I have a very close friend (we were in junior
high together in 1984) who seems to have just dropped out of society. He
doesn't look for work, having been let go from his last job. He rarely washes,
smokes and drinks too much (amongst other similar vices), and spends the time
he's not watching infomercials until 4 a.m., pining over a girl who broke up
with him long ago. He's living off unemployment, and that's going to run out
soon. 
               Oh, did I mention? He's living on my couch.
            

            
               To his credit, he's not hard to live with. He
cleans up after himself, gives me my space, and doesn't eat too much of my
food, and when he does he eventually replaces it. Plus, he's great company.
We've got very similar sense of humor and we have great conversations.

Dear Prudie,

I’ve known my closest friend since junior high, back in 1984, and over the years, he’s become like family. Lately, though, he’s fallen into a troubling pattern. He hasn’t worked since being laid off from his last job, and despite his efforts, he hasn’t been able to reenter the workforce. He rarely showers, smokes heavily, drinks excessively, and spends his nights—often well past 4 a.m.—watching infomercials while obsessively replaying memories of a girl who broke up with him years ago. He’s now living off unemployment benefits, which won’t last much longer.

To my surprise—and honestly, my dismay—he’s been staying on my couch.  

That said, I have to admit: he’s not a burden. He keeps his space clean, respects my boundaries, and even replaces the food he eats. He’s also one of the most entertaining and thoughtful people I know—our shared sense of humor and deep conversations make time with him genuinely enjoyable.  

Still, I can’t help but worry. He’s adrift, and I’m starting to feel trapped between my loyalty to him and the growing sense that I’m enabling a downward spiral. What should I do?

               Some
Feature Called "Today's Papers"
            

            I commend
the Oct. 1 Today's Papers for inserting some fun in the news with the comment
about Carleton College. The disclaimer and explanation in the next day's
Today's Papers made what was written the day before even
more humorous and fun for this reader. Keep up the good work.

               No
Amnesty for Shuger
            

            So
despite Amnesty International's reputation and 30 years experience in human
rights investigations, the Oct. 5 Today's Papers doesn't take it seriously. Why? Because its director
comes from Senegal. So much for objectivity.

            -- Gerry
Ellis London

            
               Scott
Shuger replies:
            

            
               My
question, "Where would you rather be arrested--in the U.S. or Senegal?" was
raised not as an ad hominem assessment of the Amnesty International report, but
in response to the Amnesty honcho from Senegal's comment that the U.S. criminal
justice system lagged in fairness behind (someplace he called) the world
community. Yes, there are problems with our system, and yes, there are some
countries that could teach us a thing or two about them. But my point was I
don't believe people who say most countries could--because they wouldn't prefer
to be arrested, imprisoned, tried, or sentenced in most countries.

CANDIDATE:

---

**Jen Shelton**  
Huntington, W.Va.

**A Fun Touch in the News**

I appreciate the Oct. 1 edition of *Today’s Papers* for adding a touch of humor to the news with its reference to Carleton College. The follow-up disclaimer and explanation in the next day’s column only enhanced the wit, making the original comment even more enjoyable. Keep up the excellent work.

— Sharon Johnson-Cramer  
Boston

**No Amnesty for Shuger**

Despite Amnesty International’s decades-long reputation and extensive experience in human rights advocacy, the Oct. 5 *Today’s Papers* appears to dismiss its findings—simply because the organization’s director is from Senegal. That kind of reasoning undermines objectivity and misses the point entirely.

— Gerry Ellis  
London

**Scott Shuger Responds**

My question—“Where would you rather be arrested: in the U.S. or Senegal?”—was not meant as an ad hominem attack on Amnesty International’s report. Rather, it was a response to the organization’s director, who claimed that the U.S. criminal justice system lags behind “the world community” in fairness. While I acknowledge that our system has flaws and that other nations offer valuable lessons, my broader point remains: people who argue that most countries are fairer than the U.S. would likely not actually want to be arrested, imprisoned, tried, or sentenced in most of them. The idea that fairness is universally prioritized in criminal justice is, at best, questionable.

        many residents of the Lake District. Traffic jams, overflowing car

The popularity of the Lake District is a source of considerable concern to many residents, as it brings with it a range of difficulties, including traffic jams, overflowing car parks, and eroded footpaths—challenges that are not unique to this region but are suffered by National Parks all over the world. I have long been fascinated by the way people approach the challenge of international character data exchange—not just as a technical problem, but as a broader systems issue. Having dedicated significant time and effort to this field, I feel compelled to share a concise reflection on how I now view the problem.

This text does not offer revolutionary ideas, but rather presents a fresh perspective—shaped by years of practical experience. The concepts, though expressed briefly and perhaps abstractly at first, are grounded in real-world application. They have already proven effective in the domain of 8-bit character handling: I contributed directly to the design of Kermit’s multinational 8-bit character support, and the TCP/IP network I work with is steadily adopting the principle that every character transmitted over the communication line should be ISO 8859-1 by default. Any deviation from this—such as direct EBCDIC-to-PC code translation on a single machine—is seen as harmful to interoperability, even if it offers short-term convenience.

Ultimately, progress comes not from isolated optimizations, but from aligning all components toward a shared, well-defined goal. When every piece works in concert, the collective benefit far outweighs the sum of individual gains.

And perhaps, in sharing that my native language is French—adding a layer of linguistic nuance to this brief yet complex text—I can lend it a touch of authenticity and depth, making its ideas more compelling, despite its brevity.

Navajo has long been touted by sociolinguists as a
language whose speakers maintain a great deal of language loyalty, that is, the
Navajo are reluctant to give up their heritage language. Yet the need to
establish a high-school Navajo class suggests that off the reservation, that is
exactly what young Navajo speakers are doing. The Hasidim of New York and the
Amish are two other groups known for preserving their speech--when, that is,
they maintain their social isolation from the mainstream. But once that
isolation is gone, language may soon follow.

            Cultural-loyalty movements like the class in Navajo
tend to spring up when cultural preservation is in danger, and their record of
success is not impressive. Here at the University of Illinois, we run special
sections of first- and second-year Spanish for Spanish-heritage students, and
the reason is that their Spanish is too weak to meet academic requirements.
That in turn means they may be able to speak Spanish (even that is often not
the case); but they can't read it well or write it fluently, and their grasp of
its grammar may be weak, since they haven't actually studied it as a language.
They may speak some Spanish, but they can't pass a test in it. Students also
use college language classrooms to try to recapture the heritage languages they
may have lost (for example, Hindi or Urdu), or ones they may never have
acquired (Yiddish).

CANDIDATE:
Navajo has long been celebrated by sociolinguists as a language marked by strong speaker loyalty—its communities are often reluctant to abandon their heritage language. Yet the growing need to establish high school-level Navajo language programs off the reservation suggests that many young Navajo speakers are, in fact, distancing themselves from their native tongue. Similarly, other culturally distinct groups such as the Hasidim of New York and the Amish are renowned for preserving their languages, but only so long as they remain socially isolated from the broader mainstream. Once that isolation ends, language preservation often follows suit.

Cultural-loyalty initiatives—such as heritage language classes—typically emerge when a language is under threat, yet their success rate remains limited. At the University of Illinois, for example, we offer specialized sections of first- and second-year Spanish tailored for Spanish-heritage students. The reason? Their spoken Spanish is often insufficient to meet academic standards. While some may speak the language informally, many lack the reading proficiency, writing fluency, and grammatical understanding required for academic success—because they have never formally studied Spanish as a language. As a result, they may speak some Spanish, but they cannot pass a language proficiency exam. These same classrooms also attract students seeking to reclaim heritage languages they never fully acquired—like Yiddish—or those they may have lost, such as Hindi or Urdu.

CANDIDATE:
This molecule plays a crucial role in cerebral development. MARCKS-deficient mice exhibit a high incidence of exencephaly, a high incidence of agenesis of the corpus callosum, and abnormalities in other forebrain structures. Additionally, these mice display widespread neocortical ectopias, with the findings on MARCKS-deficient mice supported by references [46, 47]. The MARCKS-related protein gene is expressed in the striatum during early brain development in the rat, as documented in reference [48]. A quantitative trait locus (QTL) modulating striatal neuron number is located in the distal part of chromosome 19 and lies in close proximity to several genes critical for telencephalic development. Among these is Vax1, a homeobox-containing gene that is a close relative of both the Emx genes and the Not genes. Vax1 is localized to the anterior ventral forebrain during development and is expressed in the striatum during embryogenesis, with its localization and expression supported by reference [28]. Vax1 plays an important role in axon guidance, and in Vax1 knockout mice, both the anterior portion of the corpus callosum and the optic chiasm are malformed or absent, as confirmed by reference [49].

I’ve known my closest friend since junior high, back in 1984, and over the years, he’s become like family. Lately, though, he’s fallen into a troubling pattern. He hasn’t worked since being laid off from his last job, and despite his efforts, he hasn’t been able to reenter the workforce. Yet as I reflect, the irony is hard to ignore. While society grapples with the horrors of violent rampages and the enduring threat of Nazism, the very tools meant to connect us are also enabling the spread of dangerous ideologies. In the same edition of the New York Times, an article by Amy Harmon titled “Internet Sale of Nazi Books in Germany Assailed” reveals how Amazon.com and Barnesandnoble.com are drawing criticism from a Los Angeles-based anti-Semitism watchdog group for shipping *Mein Kampf* into Germany—where the book remains banned.

Coincidentally, this article appears directly above an ad for a 30-day free trial of TheStreet.com. While the site likely doesn’t peddle Nazi literature, its promotion of day trading feels uncomfortably suggestive—especially given the unsettling connections between speculative finance and real-world violence, even if the precise mechanisms remain unclear. I have long been fascinated by the way people approach the challenge of international character data exchange—not just as a technical problem, but as a broader systems issue. Having dedicated significant time and effort to this field, I feel compelled to share a concise reflection on how I now view the problem.

This text does not offer revolutionary ideas, but rather presents a fresh perspective—shaped by years of practical experience. The concepts, though expressed briefly and perhaps abstractly at first, are grounded in real-world application. They have already proven effective in the domain of 8-bit character handling: I contributed directly to the design of Kermit’s multinational 8-bit character support, and the TCP/IP network I work with is steadily adopting the principle that every character transmitted over the communication line should be ISO 8859-1 by default. Any deviation from this—such as direct EBCDIC-to-PC code translation on a single machine—is seen as harmful to interoperability, even if it offers short-term convenience.

Ultimately, progress comes not from isolated optimizations, but from aligning all components toward a shared, well-defined goal. When every piece works in concert, the collective benefit far outweighs the sum of individual gains.

And perhaps, in sharing that my native language is French—adding a layer of linguistic nuance to this brief yet complex text—I can lend it a touch of authenticity and depth, making its ideas more compelling, despite its brevity.

towards the the same theory that every character on the communication

Every piece working towards a common well defined goal finally pays more

And I hope that saying that my language is French will make the ideas
in a difficult to write text even more convincing, despite being short.

In a column included in his book *Why Things Are*, Joel Achenbach explained the "three name serial killer phenomenon," a media practice of listing all three names—first, middle, and last—of individuals, particularly public figures, to minimize the risk of mistaken identity. Newspapers employ this practice to reduce the likelihood that distant cousins, high-school sweethearts, or potential employers might mistakenly believe someone with a similar name is a murderer. This precaution is especially relevant for individuals like John Kennedy Gacy and Karla Onderdunk Tucker, whose names could lead to confusion with notorious serial killers, thereby exposing them to potential lawsuits or social harm. The phrase "the John Kennedy Gacys and Karla Onderdunk Tuckers of the world" encapsulates the broader category of people vulnerable to such misidentification. While this practice is justified in many cases, the case of William Jefferson Clinton presents a notable exception: it is difficult to imagine anyone confusing him with a murderer, as illustrated by the hypothetical question, "Honey, is that guy they're impeaching the same Bill Clinton who used to sell tires over at Pep Boys?" This example underscores the improbability of mistaken identity in Clinton’s case. Randolph B. Cohen, a resident of Cambridge, Mass., wrote a letter responding to Timothy Noah’s "Chatterbox" item titled "William Jefferson Clinton," in which he agrees with the opinion—originally expressed by Noah—that three-namedness is rather unnecessary in Clinton’s case. The letter affirms that while the use of all three names serves a causal function in reducing mistaken identity and legal liability for others, it is superfluous when applied to someone as widely recognized and publicly identifiable as William Jefferson Clinton. Thus, the critique of the practice hinges on this distinction: though three names are useful in general, they are not necessary in Clinton’s specific instance, highlighting the nuanced relationship between name usage and the risk of confusion.

Navajo has long been celebrated by sociolinguists as a language marked by strong speaker loyalty—its communities are often reluctant to abandon their heritage language. Yet the growing need to establish high school-level Navajo language programs off the reservation suggests that many young Navajo speakers are, in fact, distancing themselves from their native tongue. Similarly, other culturally distinct groups such as the Hasidim of New York and the Amish are renowned for preserving their languages, but only so long as they remain socially isolated from the broader mainstream. Once that isolation ends, language preservation often follows suit.

Cultural-loyalty initiatives—such as heritage language classes—typically emerge when a language is under threat, yet their success rate remains limited. At the University of Illinois, for example, we offer specialized sections of first- and second-year Spanish tailored for Spanish-heritage students. The reason? Their spoken Spanish is often insufficient to meet academic standards. While some may speak the language informally, many lack the reading proficiency, writing fluency, and grammatical understanding required for academic success—because they have never formally studied Spanish as a language. As a result, they may speak some Spanish, but they cannot pass a language proficiency exam. These same classrooms also attract students seeking to reclaim heritage languages they never fully acquired—like Yiddish—or those they may have lost, such as Hindi or Urdu.

CANDIDATE:

language whose speakers maintain a great deal of language loyalty, that is, the
Navajo are reluctant to give up their heritage language. Yet the need to
establish a high-school Navajo class suggests that off the reservation, that is
exactly what young Navajo speakers are doing. The Hasidim of New York and the
Amish are two other groups known for preserving their speech--when, that is,
they maintain their social isolation from the mainstream. But once that
isolation is gone, language may soon follow.

            Cultural-loyalty movements like the class in Navajo
tend to spring up when cultural preservation is in danger, and their record of
success is not impressive. Here at the University of Illinois, we run special
sections of first- and second-year Spanish for Spanish-heritage students, and
the reason is that their Spanish is too weak to meet academic requirements.
That in turn means they may be able to speak Spanish (even that is often not
the case); but they can't read it well or write it fluently, and their grasp of
its grammar may be weak, since they haven't actually studied it as a language.
They may speak some Spanish, but they can't pass a test in it. Students also
use college language classrooms to try to recapture the heritage languages they
may have lost (for example, Hindi or Urdu), or ones they may never have
acquired (Yiddish).

Vax1 is localized to the anterior ventral forebrain during development and is expressed in the striatum during embryogenesis, with its localization and expression supported by reference [28]. The appearance of a new Muriel Spark novel is likened to a birth in a large artistic family, such as the Brontës, the Redgraves, the Beach Boys, or the Jackson brood—families that all run to genius and oddness. Reality and Dreams shares its build with Memento Mori, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, and A Far Cry from Kensington, and it shares many of its features and many of its gestures with each of those works. Memento Mori is a flawless exploration of mortality, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie is a flawless exploration of hero worship, and A Far Cry from Kensington is a flawless exploration of literary politics. Not every member of a distinguished family is equally appealing; Branwell Brontë, for instance, drank and raved. Reality and Dreams is not Spark's most pleasant novel, though it features Tom Richards as its hero—a filmmaker who has a passion for controlling things and trouble distinguishing between his fictions and his real life, and who does his best to manipulate both. Tom Richards is hard to warm to.

            That's the difference between ordinary altruism,
where you care about other people's happiness (though perhaps not as urgently
as you care about your own), and what I'll call "imperfect altruism," where you
reserve the right to care about how others achieve their happiness.

            We all feel altruistic toward our own future
selves. That's why we make current sacrifices for future rewards. But which
kind of altruists are we? Traditional economic theory says we're the ordinary
kind--we want to be happy in the future, though perhaps not as urgently as we
want to be happy in the present. David Laibson, a professor of political
economy at Harvard, is one of a few iconoclasts who disagree. Nobody doubts
that we are imperfectly altruistic toward others. Laibson argues that we can be
imperfectly altruistic toward ourselves. And just as imperfect altruism toward
your children can cause conflict in your family, imperfect altruism toward your

In surveying the growing number of studies and claims of new cells that can acquire some
        type of heart cell phenotype in vitro or in vivo (for a review see [6]), it will become
        increasingly important to create a set of rigorous criteria that would distinguish between
        the following: authentic progenitor cells that are already committed to the cardiac
        lineage; pluripotent stem cells that can infrequently adopt the cardiac phenotype;
        phenotypic drift of other muscle progenitors with an increased propensity to enter cardiac
        lineages; and a variety of other cell types that can aberrantly express cardiac markers
        ectopically or by fusion with neighboring cardiac muscle cells.
        Finding cell-type-specific markers for these cells will be critical, as opposed to
        generalized markers that do not allow the in vivo discrimination of their precise
        localization, mobilization, and differentiation in the intact muscle. The gold standard
        would then become the isolation of the cells from the intact organ after differentiation
        has occurred by creating genetically based or antibody-based approaches to identify and/or
        purify the already differentiated progeny from the intact muscle.

response:
As the number of studies and claims identifying new cell types capable of acquiring a cardiac cell phenotype—either in vitro or in vivo—continues to grow (see review [6]), it becomes increasingly essential to establish a rigorous set of criteria to distinguish among: (1) true cardiac progenitor cells already committed to the cardiac lineage; (2) pluripotent stem cells that rarely adopt a cardiac fate; (3) other muscle progenitors undergoing phenotypic drift with heightened potential to enter cardiac lineages; and (4) various cell types that may aberrantly express cardiac markers due to ectopic expression or cell fusion with resident cardiac muscle cells.

Identifying cell-type-specific markers will be crucial, as generalized markers often fail to enable precise in vivo tracking of a cell’s location, mobilization, and differentiation within intact cardiac tissue. The gold standard for validation should therefore involve the isolation of fully differentiated progeny directly from the intact organ, using genetically encoded or antibody-based tools to specifically identify and purify these cells after differentiation has occurred.

In surveying the growing number of studies and claims of new cells that can acquire some
        type of heart cell phenotype in vitro or in vivo (for a review see [6]), it will become
        increasingly important to create a set of rigorous criteria that would distinguish between
        the following: authentic progenitor cells that are already committed to the cardiac
        lineage; pluripotent stem cells that can infrequently adopt the cardiac phenotype;
        phenotypic drift of other muscle progenitors with an increased propensity to enter cardiac
        lineages; and a variety of other cell types that can aberrantly express cardiac markers
        ectopically or by fusion with neighboring cardiac muscle cells.
        Finding cell-type-specific markers for these cells will be critical, as opposed to
        generalized markers that do not allow the in vivo discrimination of their precise
        localization, mobilization, and differentiation in the intact muscle. The gold standard
        would then become the isolation of the cells from the intact organ after differentiation
        has occurred by creating genetically based or antibody-based approaches to identify and/or
        purify the already differentiated progeny from the intact muscle.

CANDIDATE:
As the number of studies and claims identifying new cell types capable of acquiring a cardiac cell phenotype—either in vitro or in vivo—continues to grow (see review [6]), it becomes increasingly essential to establish a rigorous set of criteria to distinguish among: (1) true cardiac progenitor cells already committed to the cardiac lineage; (2) pluripotent stem cells that rarely adopt a cardiac fate; (3) other muscle progenitors undergoing phenotypic drift with heightened potential to enter cardiac lineages; and (4) various cell types that may aberrantly express cardiac markers due to ectopic expression or cell fusion with resident cardiac muscle cells.

Identifying cell-type-specific markers will be crucial, as generalized markers often fail to enable precise in vivo tracking of a cell’s location, mobilization, and differentiation within intact cardiac tissue. The gold standard for validation should therefore involve the isolation of fully differentiated progeny directly from the intact organ, using genetically encoded or antibody-based tools to specifically identify and purify these cells after differentiation has occurred.

                  Dear
Prudie,
               
            

            
               Two of my friends
have begun taking anti-depressants. One for depression, I guess, the other to
quit smoking. Because they are on anti-depressants now, they think EVERYONE
needs them and have literally been making appointments for their whole
families! Both have told me I definitely need them. I have a professional
therapist with whom I discussed this, and she disagrees. (My therapist is not
against medication, and in fact recommends it for some patients.) When I
explained this to these two ladies, they both shook their heads--like they know
better than my therapist. One came right out and shouted that I was in denial.
Wouldn't it be nice if people restricted their opinions to those areas in which
they had professional expertise? What do you think?
            

            

               --Christine, Rochester, N.Y.
            

            Dear Chris,

            The last time Prudie
checked, girlfriends could not prescribe drugs. It is a rule of human nature
that people often, when they add or subtract something from their lives, think
everyone else should do the same. Tune out the suggestions of these amateur
shrinks. You are right that it would be nice if people only spoke of things
about which they were expert. It would also be nice if every female over the
age of 16 had a $5,000 gift certificate at Tiffany's. Alas, my dear, neither
one is likely to come to pass.
